newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish bourse seen falling next week.
newsitem.headline: Polish bourse seen falling next week.

text.p: Polish shares are seen falling next week after this week's 4.5 percent gain, as analysts said the market, with a current price-earnings ratio of 15.6, looked fairly valued at best.

"Polish firms look fairly valued," said Krzysztof Olszewski of Bank Slaski brokerage, adding that the main market, currently at 16,690.4 points, could fall toward 16,000 points next week or at best stabilise.
Analysts were not sure the market had put all of its recent profit-taking correction behind it after having surged to a three-year high at 18,339.4 points on February 18.
Analysts were cheered the market had survived the U.S.'s 25-basis-point Funds rate rise on Tuesday but said this did not necessarily provide a platform for growth.
"The fact the rise has been discounted does not mean that a long period of growth awaits us," said Pawel Tarnowski, an analyst at Raiffeisen Capital and Investment.

Tarnowski said prospective earnings for many listed firms this year did not warrant much buying at current price levels and that the Polish bourse should continue to perform in line with major foreign exchanges, which could see falls.

Analysts also said the recent underperformance by banks, which make up about 40 percent of the main index, was caused by recent slower earnings growth compared to other heavyweights and was keeping the main index down.
They said that as a result smaller speculative stocks were leading the market, such as debt-ridden Espebepe, which surged 41.9 percent this week after last week's 46.4 percent plunge.
The builder's creditors meet on April 14 to discuss a possible restructuring of its 75 million zlotys in debt.

Analysts said Polifarb Cieszyn, the only large-cap stock among this week's top gainers, could continue this week's 19.8-percent rise if investors remain confident in its planned merger with Polifarb Wroclaw.
Wroclaw rose only 1.3 percent this week, tumbling on Wednesday after the firms' shareholders agreed on a merger, with Cieszyn's approving a plan giving themselves 53.5 percent.
Wroclaw officials have said a mutual shareholder, BIG, might dispute Cieszyn's version in court but that the merger was still likely to go through as a delay would cost both firms.
On Thursday a Wroclaw shareholder said it and other Western investment funds had asked the Polish Securities Commission to prevent Cieszyn's version of the merger.
